Appendix B: Fraction of total resources allocated to the largest training run

When modeling electrical power and chip manufacturing capacity, we must consider how competition between AI labs affects the fraction of these resources that a lab can secure to perform the largest training run. To estimate this fraction, we consider the stock of AI chips available to each of the most well-resourced firms at the beginning of 2024. We then divide each firm’s stock by the total stock of AI chips available. Finally, we adjust this fraction down to account for some chips being allocated to inference. For convenience, we measure the stock of AI chips in terms of H100-equivalents: the number of Nvidia H100 GPUs that would match the total FLOP/s of the stock, at 16-bit precision. Full calculations are available here.

Meta: According to analyst firm Omdia, Meta acquired 150,000 H100 GPUs by the end of 2023. Meta plans to have a total of 600,000 H100-equivalent GPUs by the end of 2024. So it is likely that Meta’s stock of H100-equivalents at the beginning of 2024 was between 150,000 and 600,000.

Microsoft: Omdia estimates that Microsoft also acquired 150,000 H100 GPUs by the end of 2023. Microsoft reportedly plans to triple their stock of AI chips to 1.8 million by December. It is unclear what kind of chips these will be, but the plan implies that the initial stock was 600,000 chips, and the timing suggests that many of the new chips will be H100s. Based on the rate of hardware efficiency improvements, the initial stock of 600,000 chips would equate to around 300,000 H100 equivalents.105 However, it is unclear exactly when Microsoft’s expansion plans started. Microsoft may have already acquired more H100 GPUs by the start of 2024; we estimate up to 140,000.106 Accounting for all of this, we believe that Microsoft’s stock of H100-equivalents at the beginning of 2024 was likely between 150,000 and 600,000.

Google: Little is known publicly about the production of Google’s custom AI chips, known as TPUs. However, one report by analyst firm TechInsights estimates the total number of TPU shipments each year.107 Based on the release dates of each generation of TPU, it is likely that most of the estimated 2 million units in 2023 and 1.5 million units in 2022 were TPUv5. However, there are two versions of TPUv5: the more efficient TPUv5e, and the higher-performance TPUv5p. The share of each TPU type is unclear, so we estimate the total number of TPUv5 units shipped to be between 1 and 3.5 million, and the share of that total made up by TPUv5p to be between 10% and 90%.

As for TPUv4, which was released in 2021, we believe that peak production likely occurred between 2020 and 2022, and estimate that a total of 250,000 to 1.5 million units were produced based on the yearly production reported by TechInsights. We neglect older generations of TPU, given the much lower estimates of production prior to 2021 and the lower performance of those older generations. Google also owns Nvidia GPUs, but given the track record of Google labs exclusively using TPUs to train their flagship models, we think it is unlikely they will allocate these GPUs to their largest training run. So putting the TPUv4 and TPUv5 numbers together, we estimate that the total number of H100-equivalents available to Google is between 400,000 and 1.4 million.

Amazon: According to the Omdia report, Amazon acquired 50,000 H100 GPUs by the end of 2023, which is three times less than Microsoft and Meta. Amazon also has custom Trainium chips, with one report that Amazon Web Services (AWS) will soon offer clusters of up to 100,000 Trainium2 chips with a peak of 65e18 FLOP/s of compute. This corresponds to about 66,000 H100-equivalents assuming FP16 precision, or 33,000 assuming FP8 precision. If Amazon already has several of these clusters, they may have hundreds of thousands of H100-equivalents in total. Given that these clusters are only just coming online, however, it seems unlikely that Amazon’s stock of AI chips would exceed Google’s estimated stock of 400,000 to 1.4 million H100-equivalents.

Total stock: To estimate the total stock of AI chips available for training by the beginning of 2024, we add up actual H100s shipped, other GPUs, and Google TPUs. The actual H100s shipped was likely between 500,000 and 1.6 million. Omdia estimated a total of 650,000 shipped to major companies. Given Nvidia’s annualized data center revenue of $47.5 billion, and a price of $30,000, they could only have sold about 1.6 million H100s at most.

Other GPUs likely make up between 200,000 and 1 million H100 equivalents. The peak years for the previous generation A100 were 2021 and 2022, in which Nvidia earned a combined $25 billion in data center revenue. At $15,000 per unit, this implies at most 1.7 million units sold, corresponding to about 500,000 H100 equivalents. A more conservative estimate would be $15B / $20,000 ~= 750,000 A100s—roughly 250,000 H100 equivalents. Besides the A100, other GPUs would have a smaller contribution, as they either have lower performance or a much smaller share of the market. Above, we estimated that Microsoft’s 150,000 H100 GPUs imply roughly double that number in total H100 equivalents; a similar argument here implies at most 500,000 * 2 = 1 million H100 equivalents from non-H100 GPUs.

Training allocation: Available computing resources are split between training new models and running inference on existing ones. A simple analysis suggests AI labs should allocate comparable resources to both tasks. Assuming this balance, we can estimate future resource allocation. If in 2029 training and inference compute are equal, and training compute continues to grow at 4x per year, one-quarter of total compute (equal to 2029’s training) will run inference on 2029 models, while three-quarters will train 2030 models. This suggests that 80% of 2030’s compute would be used for training new models, while 20% would be used for inference on previous models.

Result: Adding the stock of actual H100s, other GPUs, and TPUs together results in an estimate of 1.5 to 3.5 million H100-equivalents in total by the beginning of 2024. Since Google has the highest stock estimate of 400,000 to 1.4 million H100-equivalents, we use this stock to estimate the allocation of total resources. After adjusting for 80% of a company’s compute being spent on training, our final result is that the largest training run can be allocated 26% (somewhere between 16% to 40%) of the total available chip stock.

Appendix C: Bandwidth constraints

Suppose we have a ring all-reduce setup involving \(M\) data centers, with fiber optic bandwidth \(F\) bps between every data pair and \(t\_L\) seconds of latency for a round trip across the network.

The standard all-ring reduce includes \(M-1\) stages of parallel reduce followed by \(M-1\) stages of broadcast. In each stage, peers communicate to their next neighbor a tensor of size \(N/M\), where \(N\) is the size of the model, which can be communicated in  \(N/M \times 8 / F\) seconds, assuming 8 bits per parameter. In total, this takes \(2(M-1) \times N/M \times 8 / F \approx 2 \times N \times 8 / F\) seconds.

To this we need to add the latency, corresponding to two round trips down the network, for a total time per all reduce of:

\[ t\_{\text{AR}} = \frac{2 \times N \times 8}{F} + 2 \times t\_L \]

Following a logic similar to what is explained in the section Feasibility of distributed training runs when talking about latencies, this would lead to a maximum of \(U = \frac{T}{t\_{\text{AR}}}\) gradient updates, allowing for a dataset size of \(D = U \times B\) , where \(B\) is the maximum achievable batch size.

We assume the usual Chinchilla relation between model size and number of parameters (\(D = 20 \times N\)), and numerically solve for the largest model that can be trained using the fsolve facility in scipy.

Appendix D: Equivalence between multimodal and text data

Here we set out to estimate how many tokens an image or second of video would be encoded as, in relation to one token of text.

Establishing an equivalence rate between data of different modalities is complex. In the limit, we expect multimodal tokenizers to encode media with an amount of tokens roughly proportional to the amount of information therein contained. So we try to estimate how much information image and video data have in relation to text.

Henighan et al (2020) estimate that one 32x32 image provides an information gain over a description as the equivalent of 2-3 words (eg 2-4 tokens of text), which we take as a lower bound on the information content of an image. Chameleon-34B encode 512x512 images using 1024 text-equivalent tokens, i.e. 770 words. As of June 2024, OpenAI charges 255 text tokens to process 512x512 images with GPT-4o. Yu et al (2023) encode images with good performance using 256 tokens with a dictionary of 218 tokens, four times bigger than typical text tokenizers; we take that as equivalent to \(256 \times 18/16 \approx 290\) text tokens (typical text tokenizers use a codebook with 216 entries, hence the adjustment). Yu et al (2024) encodes 256x256 images using 32 tokens from a codebook with 211 entries, equivalent to \(32 \times \frac{11}{16} = 22\) text tokens. While the Chameleon paper is the most straightforward application, given the rest of the evidence pointing towards lower dimensions we consider a range of 2 to 290 tokens per image.

For video, we speculate that one second of video content would be the equivalent of 2-10 words of content based on typical speech speeds, i.e. 2-13 text tokens. The information in a video is highly redundant compared to images—for instance, typical high res images take up 2MB of space, while 720p/1080p videos take up 1GB of space per hour of video, ie 0.2MB per second of video, which would suggest there is less information per second of video than in ten images. So we take as lower bound the 2 tokens per second of speech and as an upper bound the same 290 tokens per second that we assigned to an image, as a generous upper bound of the image content in the video.

Thus we arrive at a rate of 2 to 290 tokens per image or second of video. We consider this an extremely rough guess, and acknowledge there is significant room for disagreement.

Appendix E: Computing the largest possible training run given variable communication latency restrictions

In this appendix we explain how we estimate the largest model that can be trained using a tree topology setup without running into latency constraints.

The latency per layer and batch \(t\_L\) corresponds to combining the base comms latency \(t\_{\text{base}}\) and the variable comms latencies within a node \(t\_{\text{INTRA}}\)  and across nodes \(t\_{\text{INTER}}\). Here we are assuming 8-GPU NVLINK nodes (of which at most \(\lceil \sqrt 8 \rceil = 3\) coordinate after each layer), and a tree structure, using the formula for an all-reduce latency found in the NCCL repository. We multiply this by 4 since each layer has an attention and MLP block, which need to be traversed forward and backward for each batch during training.

\[ t\_L = 4 \times \left[t\_{\text{base}} + 2 \times \left(t\_{\text{INTRA}} \times 3 + t\_{\text{INTER}} \times \max\left(0, \log\_2\left(\frac{\text{TP}\_\text{RANK-2D}}{8}\right)\right)\right)\right] \]

The number of ranks involved in 2D tensor parallelism synchronization after each layer (\(\text{TP}\\_\text{RANK-2D}\)) is the square root of the number of ranks involved in tensor parallelism overall. We bound this as inversely proportional to the maximum slicing across GPUs that can be achieved with data and pipeline parallelism, considering the minimum number of samples in a batch \(B\_{\text{MIN}}\) that can be processed with TP efficiently (\( DP\_\text{RANK} \times PP\_\text{RANK} = \frac{B}{ B\_{\text{MIN}}}  \)).

\[ \text{TP}\_\text{RANK-2D} = \max\left(1, \sqrt{\frac{n\_{\text{gpu}} \cdot B\_{\text{MIN}}}{B}}\right) \]

To estimate \(B\_{\text{MIN}}\) in the first place we need to look into the utilization that GPUs can achieve given their bandwidth. This utilization is optimized when the amount of time spent on memory accesses is roughly equal to the time spent on computation. For language transformers, we will be multiplying tensors with dimensions \((B\_{\text{MIN}}, d\_{\text{ff}}, d\_{\text{model}})\), which roughly require \(B\_{\text{MIN}} \times d\_{\text{model}} \times d\_{\text{ff}}\) multiply-adds and  \(B\_{\text{MIN}} \cdot d\_{\text{model}} + d\_{\text{model}} \cdot d\_{\text{ff}} + B\_{\text{MIN}} \cdot d\_{\text{ff}}\) read-writes, where dff and dmodel  are the feed-forward and model dimensions respectively. Assuming a peak hardware performance of H FLOP/s, a bandwidth of W bytes/s and a parameter precision of p bytes, the equilibrium between memory access and computation will be achieved when:

\[ \frac{2 \text{ FLOP/multiply-add} \times \# \text{ multiply-adds}}{H} = \frac{\# \text{read-writes} \times p}{W} \]\[ \frac{2 \times B\_{\text{MIN}} \times d\_{\text{model}} \times d\_{\text{ff}}}{H} = \frac{(B\_{\text{MIN}} \times d\_{\text{model}} + d\_{\text{model}} \times d\_{\text{ff}} + B\_{\text{MIN}} \times d\_{\text{ff}}) \times p}{W} \]\[ \frac{2 \times W}{H \times p} = \frac{1}{B\_{\text{MIN}}} + \frac{1}{d\_{\text{model}}} + \frac{1}{d\_{\text{ff}}} \]

For a sufficiently large model, the right side of this equation simplifies to \(1 / B\_{\text{MIN}}\), and we have that:

\[ B\_{\text{MIN}} = \frac{H \times p}{2 \times W} \]

For the H100 at FP8 precision, the minimum batch size per GPU would then correspond to \(B\_{\text{MIN}} = \frac{2e15 \text{ FLOP/s} \times 1 \text{ byte/param}}{2 \text{ FLOP/multiply-add} \times 3e12 \text{ bytes/s}} \approx 330\). Theoretically, this minimum batch size would increase over time, as the bandwidth and hardware performance improve unequally fast. For simplicity of the analysis, we assume that it will stay roughly fixed.

The number of GPUs is approximated by the model compute \(C\) divided by the training duration \(T\) and the utilization-adjusted hardware performance \( H \) (this is an underestimate, as utilization worsens with scale).

\[N\_{\text{GPU}} = C(T \times H)\]

The model compute \(C\), dataset size \(D\) and model size \(N\) obey the usual relation.

\[C = 6DN\]

And dataset size \(D\) is assumed to scale in relation to model size \(N\) following the Chinchilla rule.

\[D = 20 \times N\]

The batch size \(B\) and the layer depth \(L\) are assumed to grow exponentially with respect to model size (if assuming that batch size doesn’t scale then just take \(B\) as given).

\[B = B\_0 \times N^\alpha\_B\]\[L = L\_0 \times N^\alpha\_L\]

The minimum training time \(T\) is then bounded by time per layer and batch size \(t\_L\) times the number of layers \(L\) times the number of gradient updates (\(U = D/B\)). In the point where scale is maximized, this limit will be taut.

\[T = t\_L \times L \times D/B\]

We solve this system of equations numerically using the fsolve facility in scipy.

Appendix F: Unprecedented economic growth could drive massive AI investment

In the section “Will labs attempt to scale to these new heights?”, we argued that the unprecedented economic growth from AI automation could drive massive AI investments. While this is far from guaranteed, in this appendix we outline a rough calculation to illustrate this dynamic.

The starting point is to consider a lifetime value function \(V\), with isoelastic flow utility over consumption \(c\). To capture the economic impact of massive AI automation, we assume that consumption is constant at \(\bar{c}\) until some year \(T\), after which consumption goes to infinity. We then have

\[V(c,T) = -\sum\_{t=0}^T \beta^t \bar{c}^{-\gamma} = -\bar{c}^{-\gamma} \frac{1-\beta^{T+1}}{1-\beta},\]

where we sum over years \(t\) with discount \(\beta\) and elasticity of intertemporal substitution \(\gamma\).

The next step is to relate this to AI investment – in particular, we consider how much flow consumption a representative agent would be willing to bring forward the arrival date of these economic impacts. Let’s say the representative agent is indifferent between a consumption of \(c\_1\) in year \(T\_1\) and a consumption of \(c\_2\) in year \(T\_2\), i.e. \(V(c\_1, T\_1) = V(c\_2, T\_2)\). Then it follows that

\[ \frac{c\_1}{c\_2} = \left(\frac{1-\beta^{T\_1+1}}{1-\beta^{T\_2+1}}\right)^{\frac{1}{\gamma}}\]

With this expression, we can now plug in some plausible numbers for illustration. Suppose we want to move the point of massive automation from \(T\_2 = 30\) years to \(T\_1 = 20\) years, with a discount rate of 2% (i.e. \(\beta = 0.98\)) and \(\gamma = 1\) (Havránek et al. 2015). Then we have \(\frac{c\_1}{c\_2} \approx 0.74\), implying that it is worth giving up 26% of flow consumption each year!

In the US, around 70-80% of GDP is dedicated to consumption (World Bank, 2022), amounting to around $18.75T each year. If we believe the above calculation, this suggests forfeiting around $4.7T worth of consumption annually to hasten the arrival of massive automation. Of course, this calculation is based on aggressive assumptions, but at the very least it illustrates why massive upfront investments in AI infrastructure might make sense.

Meanwhile, McKinsey estimates US data centers consumed 17 GW on average in 2022, and Goldman Sachs estimates 146 TWh in 2023, or ~17 GW on average. Given this range of estimates, and rapid growth in recent years, the current rate is likely above 20 GW.

SemiAnalyis reports the critical IT capacity (see Figure 2) without accounting for power usage effectiveness (PUE), which is total data center power divided by power used directly for compute rather than overhead functions such as cooling. Our estimate of power consumption per GPU also includes this overhead, so we need to use the total capacity, not the IT capacity. We arrive at our estimates of 36 GW and 48 GW by assuming a PUE of 1.5x for non-AI data centers, and a PUE of 1.2x for AI data centers, based on SemiAnalysis estimates.

Another projection from a grid operator is that Dominion’s data center load will grow by 4x over 15 years, and 4^(1/15) = ~1.1, or 10% growth. The shorter-term projection is likely more relevant since we are discussing growth until 2030.

Recent annual growth in non-AI IT capacity in North America according to SemiAnalysis data was between 11% to 13%.

Our best guess is that Google currently has the largest share, at 33% (20% to 50%). See Appendix B for further details. It’s possible that some companies might choose to reserve a substantial fraction of their resources for inference; here we implicitly assume they will dedicate a majority of their resources to a training cluster, which later might be reused for inference.

Modern ethernet switches like Marvell’s Teralynx 10 have latencies in the order of 500 ns per packet forward, which can be ignored in comparison to the much larger flight latencies.

The historical trend would suggest 600 Tbps / 128 ports = 5 Tbps by the end of the decade, which is roughly congruent with the expert assessment, suggesting that the trend can in fact be continued up to this point.

Companies seeking to scale up power very aggressively may have high discount rates and prefer gas for that reason.

This suggests that 80% of 2030’s compute would be used for training new models, while 20% would be used for inference on last year’s models.

  76. What if we are training sparse models, such as mixture-of-expert architectures? Sparsity allows to greatly reduce the number of parameters involved in each forward pass. If the number of tokens used for training roughly follows Chinchilla scaling we would then expect data stocks to become fully utilized at lower compute scales, by at least as much as 10x given typical sparsity levels. However, scaling laws for sparse models are poorly understood—efficiently trained models might be trained on less data. For the time being we ignore this consideration.

Once AI labs run into a training data bottleneck, they can still train larger models without increasing the dataset size to increase performance, at a reduced efficiency – this is known as undertraining. For example, if the loss follows the Chinchilla parametric fit one might be able to undertrain models by a factor of up to 3000x with the loss gradient only reducing by a factor of 10x with respect to Chinchilla scaling. Similarly, AI labs might choose to overtrain models to increase the efficiency at inference time (as this allows to reach similar performance with smaller models). Overtraining might cause AI labs to run into data bottlenecks sooner. For simplicity, we set aside undertraining and overtraining considerations.

We account for this in our final estimates, but given its small significance we elide it in the discussion.

(While traffic and content are not the same thing, they are likely well correlated.) Lee (2021) reports that worldwide image capture is in the order of ~1T/year, so the stock will likely be close to ~10T images total.

A large source of mostly untranscribed audio are podcasts: the Podcast Index has indexed 143 million podcast episodes or about 350B seconds of audio at an average duration of ~40 minutes per episode. Music is likely the least redundant type of audio data, and Spotify contains 100 million songs, corresponding to about 24B seconds of music. Overall, it seems likely that there are on the order of hundreds of billions of seconds of publicly available, non-redundant audio.

A target model trained with tenfold as much compute would have \(\sqrt{10}\) times as many parameters, and so would take \(6 \times \sqrt{10} \times N\) FLOP to process a datapoint during training. Generating that data point would require \(10 \times 2N\) FLOP using the initial model with \(N\) parameters and exploiting the inference-training tradeoff over a \(\text{10x}\) training gap. Therefore, the ratio between the compute used for generation and training on each datapoint is \(\frac{10 \times 2N \text{ FLOP}}{6 \times  \sqrt{10} \times N \text{ FLOP}} = \frac{\sqrt{10}}{3} \approx 1\).

This occurs with small matrices, and we in fact expect this to be more binding on current hardware than the latency bottleneck. It is unclear how the balance between memory bandwidth and hardware performance will evolve in the future.

  93. The NCCL repository indicates a base latency of 6.8 µs, and a variable NVLINK ring latency of 0.6 µs per rank and round of communication. In a typical NVLINK configuration one would have 8 GPUs, of which 2-3 talk per matmul for 2D tensor parallelism purposes. So the latency per communication per all-reduce is \(6.8\,\mu\text{s} + 2 \times (3-1) \times 0.6\,\mu\text{s} = 9.2\,\mu\text{s}\), since an all-reduce requires two rounds of communication.

For instance, Erdil and Schneider-Joseph (2024) calculate that Hoffmann et al (2022) scale their models as \( L = 8.8e{-2}\, N^{0.27} \), where \(L\) is the number of layers and \(N\) is the number of parameters. Note that there is little existing work on “shape” scaling laws, so we are significantly uncertain about whether this relation will hold in the future.

To step through the calculation: The training time \( T \) must be less than nine months, and is at least as high as the induced latency \(t\_L \times L \times D/B\), where \(t\_L\) is the minimal latency per layer and batch, L is the number of layers and \(D/B\) is the number of batches processed (dataset size \(D\) divided by batch size \(B\)). Solving \( T > t\_L \times L \times D/B \) with the scaling assumptions \( L = 8.8e{-2}\, N^{0.27} \) and \(D = 20N\) results in \( N < [\frac{T\times B}{20 \cdot t\_L \cdot 8.8e{-2}}]^{1/1.27} \) (\(N\) is the number of model parameters). This results in a maximum model size of 700T parameters, which following Chinchilla scaling would allow a training run of \(C = 6DN = 6 \cdot 20 N^2 = 6e31\) FLOP.

We can model the all-reduce latency involving \(M\) pods and \(N\) GPUs per pod as \(t = t\_{\text{KERNEL}} + t\_{\text{BASE}} + 2 \times \left(3 \times t\_{\text{INTRA}} + \log\_2(N) \times t\_{\text{INTER}}\right)\). We have values \(t\_{\text{BASE}} = 6.8\,\mu\text{s}, \quad t\_{\text{INTRA}} = 0.6\,\mu\text{s}, \quad t\_{\text{INTER}} = 5\,\mu\text{s}\) for values of the base, intranode (NVLINK) and internode (InfiniBand) latencies in the low latency (LL) tree setup described in the NCCL repository, plus a \(t\_{\text{KERNEL}} = 4.5,\mu\text{s}\) kernel latency as in Erdil and Schneider-Joseph (2024).

About the authors

Jaime Sevilla
Jaime Sevilla is the co-founder and Chief Executive Officer of Epoch AI. His research is focused on technological forecasting and the trajectory of AI. He has a background in Mathematics and Computer Science.
Tamay Besiroglu
Tamay Besiroglu co-founded Epoch AI and remains contributing to the organization as a research advisor. He left Epoch to co-lead Mechanize, a startup building virtual work environments, benchmarks, and training data for AI development. His research expertise focuses on the economics of computing and broader trends in machine learning.
Ben Cottier
Ben Cottier is a senior researcher at Epoch AI. He leads the AI data centers project. Besides data centers, Ben is interested in AI cost trends and the diffusion of AI capabilities. He previously worked as a software engineer, and has a masters degree in AI from the University of Edinburgh.
Josh You
Josh You is a researcher who collects and analyzes data on AI systems. Before Epoch AI, he worked as a software engineer and a content writer, and graduated from Carleton College with a degree in Computer Science and Mathematics.
Edu Roldán
Edu Roldán is a software engineer at Epoch AI. He helps maintain the website and assists researchers with programming tasks.
Pablo Villalobos
Pablo Villalobos has a background in Mathematics and Computer Science. After spending some time as a software engineer, he decided to pivot towards AI. His interests include the economic consequences of advanced AI systems and the role of algorithmic improvements in AI progress.
Ege Erdil
Ege Erdil is a former researcher at Epoch AI. He has interests in mathematics, statistics, economics and forecasting.

Can AI scaling continue through 2030?

We investigate four constraints to scaling AI training: power, chip manufacturing, data, and latency. We predict 2e29 FLOP runs will be feasible by 2030.
